reader_question: How do the three kinds of federal trial judges differ: district, bankruptcy and magistrate judges?
grade_line: Documented: title 28 of the U.S. Code, as in force on November 12, 2026, with seats as the federal courts counted them on September 30, 2025
title: District judges hold office for life once the President appoints them and the Senate consents, and other judges choose bankruptcy and magistrate judges for terms of 14 years and eight years.
measure_line: Who appoints each kind of federal trial judge, with whose consent, for how long, what cases they hear, how many seats there are and who sets that number, from 28 U.S.C. 133, 134, 152, 631 and 633 and the federal courts’ count
notes: Seats include vacant ones. The law’s own tables list 673 district judgeships and 316 bankruptcy judgeships, and the Judicial Conference sets the number of magistrate judges.
alt: Three cards compare district, bankruptcy and magistrate judges on who appoints them, for how long, what they hear and how many seats there are.

table.caption: The three kinds of federal trial judges

columns.label: Judgeships the law’s table lists
columns.empty: None; set by the Judicial Conference

notes.1: Includes four in the territorial district courts of Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and the Virgin Islands, whose judges serve ten-year terms.
